limits: Monitoring supports PostgreSQL 14 and newer; DBLab supports PostgreSQL 10 and newer.
Monitoring needs the pg_stat_statements extension. Wait events are sampled from pg_stat_activity, not traced.
Starter covers the primary node only, keeps 14 days of history, and has no Grafana dashboards and no included expert requests.
DBLab SE is limited to 2,000 GiB per instance and a single user.
All DBLab clones share one machine, and copy-on-write storage has different I/O performance, so timings on a clone should not be compared directly with production.
Managed services such as Amazon RDS are copied to DBLab with dump and restore and refreshed in full; the first copy of a source is slow, about 1 TiB an hour.

facts.text: PostgresAI monitoring shows its dashboards in Grafana. A self-hosted install keeps the metrics on your own infrastructure.
PostgresAI monitoring comes with pre-built Grafana dashboards; on hosted plans Grafana comes with Scale.
The Console has a PostgresAI Assistant, in beta.
DBLab Engine runs on a single machine, with Docker and a ZFS or LVM volume.
A DBLab clone is an ordinary PostgreSQL server that any Postgres client can connect to.
Reset returns a DBLab clone to its snapshot.
DBLab 4.0 and later has branches and snapshots (dblab commit).
DBLab 4.2 adds an in-place major version upgrade of a single clone and retention policies for branches and snapshots.

Logical mode, the only mode for managed services such as Amazon RDS, gets fresh data by full refresh. With one disk this needs a maintenance window and removes existing clones; with several pools it refreshes without downtime (4.0 and later).
For Amazon RDS and Aurora, the refresh can dump from a temporary RDS clone, leaving production untouched (4.1 and later).
Physical mode keeps a continuously updated copy of a self-managed source.
Joe runs EXPLAIN on DBLab clones and is available in Slack, a web UI and the CLI (pgai joe).
The express checkup in the postgresai CLI runs from a terminal against PostgreSQL 14 or newer; with --no-upload it needs no account and sends no report data to PostgresAI.

monitoring.label: PostgresAI vs monitoring, observability and AI tuning tools
monitoring.intro: PostgresAI monitors PostgreSQL, runs scheduled health checkups and turns findings into Issues that you, your AI agent or a PostgresAI expert can act on. These pages compare it with other tools that watch, diagnose or tune Postgres.

groups.label: AI tuning and AI DBA tools

rows.label: What it is
rows.us: PostgreSQL monitoring with scheduled health checkups. Findings become Issues with severity, evidence and a recommended fix, which you, your AI agent or a PostgresAI expert can act on.

rows.label: Where your Postgres can run, and which versions
rows.us: Amazon RDS and Aurora, Google Cloud SQL, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Supabase, Tiger Data, self-managed servers and Postgres running on Kubernetes. PostgreSQL 14 and newer, with the pg_stat_statements extension.

rows.label: Where it runs and what it collects
rows.us: Hosted by PostgresAI, or self-hosted in your own cloud account or on your own server. It collects database metadata such as statistics, normalized query texts and wait events, not table data or query parameters.

rows.label: Open source
rows.us: The monitoring software is open source under Apache 2.0. Hosted plans are a separate paid service.

rows.label: Query performance analysis
rows.us: Top queries from pg_stat_statements by calls, execution time, planning time and rows, with a drill-down dashboard for a single query. For execution plans, Joe runs EXPLAIN on a DBLab clone.

rows.label: Wait event analysis
rows.us: An ASH-style wait event dashboard built from samples of pg_stat_activity. No extra extension is needed.

rows.label: Health checks and recommendations
rows.us: Scheduled checkup reports on settings, autovacuum and bloat, and indexes (invalid, unused, redundant). Each finding becomes an Issue with severity, evidence and a specific fix.

rows.label: AI and agent access
rows.us: The postgresai CLI (alias pgai) and an MCP server with tools for Issues, action items and checkup reports. The setup guide covers Cursor, Claude Code, Windsurf and Codex.

rows.label: Testing a fix before production
rows.us: With DBLab Engine, a separate open-source product: a full-size thin clone of the database in seconds, where an index or query change can be run on real data. DBLab is set up and priced separately.

branching.label: DBLab vs database branching, cloning and test data tools
branching.intro: DBLab Engine gives every developer, CI job and AI agent a full-size, writable copy of a PostgreSQL database in seconds, from any Postgres source, on a machine you control. These pages compare it with other ways to get a copy to test on.

groups.label: Branching built into a Postgres platform
Branching for a database hosted elsewhere
Database virtualization and test data products

rows.label: What it is
rows.us: Open-source software that gives every developer, CI job and AI agent a writable, full-size copy of a PostgreSQL database in seconds. Thin clones share one physical copy of the data on one machine.

rows.label: Which databases it can copy
rows.us: Any PostgreSQL from version 10 up, wherever it runs. Managed services such as Amazon RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL and Supabase are copied with dump and restore; self-managed servers can also be copied physically with WAL-G, pgBackRest or pg_basebackup.

rows.label: How a copy is made
rows.us: Copy-on-write in the file system, with ZFS or LVM. Clones share unchanged blocks, so a clone takes extra disk space only for what it changes.

rows.label: Time to get a copy
rows.us: A few seconds whatever the database size: under 2 seconds for a 10 TiB database with one user, up to 30 seconds with 15 users at once. The first copy of the source is slow; about 1 TiB an hour is a good speed.

rows.label: Data in a copy
rows.us: The whole database as of the chosen snapshot. Physical mode can follow the source continuously; logical mode is refreshed in full, on a schedule.

rows.label: Masking sensitive data
rows.us: Documented options: load an anonymized dump, or apply SQL transformations or PostgreSQL Anonymizer before snapshots are taken. You define the rules.

rows.label: CI and migration testing
rows.us: DB Migration Checker runs pending migrations on a clone in CI, fails those that hold dangerous locks longer than a limit (10 seconds by default) and collects statistics. Any CI job can also create clones through the API or CLI.

rows.label: API, CLI and agent access
rows.us: REST API, web UI and the dblab CLI. Joe, also available as pgai joe, returns EXPLAIN plans and timings from a clone, not rows.

rows.label: Where it runs
rows.us: On a machine you control, in any cloud or on-premises. DBLab SE installs from the PostgresAI Console or AWS Marketplace.

rows.label: Open source
rows.us: DBLab Engine is open source under Apache 2.0.

rows.label: Documented limits
rows.us: DBLab SE: 2,000 GiB per instance and a single user. All clones share one machine, and copy-on-write storage has different I/O performance, so timings on a clone should not be compared directly with production.

usSources.title: Query timing on clones and in production

rows.label: What you pay for
rows.us: One machine and one physical copy of the data, however many clones run. DBLab SE is billed hourly by the size of that machine, not by database size or number of clones.

changes.label: DBLab and schema change tools
changes.intro: Schema change tools write, review and deploy migrations. DBLab runs a migration on a full-size clone first and measures how long it takes and which locks it holds. They complement each other; these pages show where each one stops.

rows.label: What it is
rows.us: Thin clones of a full-size PostgreSQL database, used to run a schema change on real data before it ships. DBLab does not write, order or deploy migrations.

rows.label: Runs the change on full-size data
rows.us: DB Migration Checker applies pending migrations to a full-size clone in CI and collects statistics from the run.

rows.label: Lock and downtime risk
rows.us: Measured on the clone: the checker fails a migration that holds a dangerous lock longer than a limit, 10 seconds by default.

rows.label: Static review and lint rules
rows.us: None. DBLab runs the change; it does not lint SQL.

rows.label: Writing, versioning and deploying migrations
rows.us: Not provided. Keep your migration tool; a clone is an ordinary PostgreSQL server that any tool can connect to.

rows.label: Approvals and audit trail
rows.us: Not a change-approval system. DBLab EE adds SSO, user management and audit for access to clones.

rows.label: Rollback
rows.us: Not provided for production. On a clone, reset returns the data to the snapshot, so a migration can be run again.
